::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
**Section 5 is filled and Phase 0 is done.** The site was crawled from a local
machine on 2026-09-01: eleven pages, nineteen linked files, none of them hosted
on the old site. Section 7 still describes the Google Takeout route, which the
crawl makes unnecessary, and Sections 8 and 11 were written expecting hosted
files to rescue. Those three sections need revising against Section 5. What
Sections 3, 4, 9 and 10 decide is unaffected.
:::

## In brief

**The goal.** One site, at one URL, holding both what is now on
`sites.google.com/site/andrewsteinphd` and what is now on TrinityMetrics, with
no content dropped without a recorded decision to drop it.

**The two sites are about different things.** The Google site is about a
person: bio, publications, talks, software, contact. TrinityMetrics is about a
subject. Merging them means the merged site has to answer two questions on
arrival, "who is this" and "what is this for", and the navigation has to make
both findable without either burying the other.

**Decision on naming.** The site stays TrinityMetrics, at the
`trinitymetrics.com` address Andy already holds, and the personal material
becomes a section rather than the site's title. Section 3 argues this against
the two alternatives.

**Decision on the subject.** Three legs: pharmacometrics, teaching and
education, GenAI, in that order. Teaching is how someone learns to make a
defensible quantitative claim, pharmacometrics is making them, and GenAI is
what happens to both when producing a plausible claim becomes cheap. Section 3
records what this rejects and why.

**Recommendation on placement.** Person-level pages become top-level
(`publications.qmd`, `talks.qmd`), grouped in the navbar under one menu with
the CV as a link out to Google Docs; the existing `about.qmd` becomes the
person's landing page and stops being a project description. Section 4 maps
every kind of content.

**Files and old URLs.** A Google Site's PDFs, slides and images live at URLs
that stop existing when the site does, and those URLs are cited from CVs,
papers and conference bios that cannot be edited. Section 8 and Section 11
cover this, and it is the reason the old site should be kept alive as a set of
pointers rather than deleted.

**Where to start.** Phase 0: export the site and fill in Section 5. Every other
decision here gets easier once the actual page and file list exists, and two of
the open questions in Section 14 may answer themselves.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## 1. Scope

In scope: every page, file and link currently reachable from
`sites.google.com/site/andrewsteinphd`, and the changes to this repository
needed to hold them.

Out of scope, stated once:

-   **A visual redesign.** The merged site uses the existing `cosmo` theme and
    `styles.css`. If the merge makes a design problem obvious, record it and
    handle it separately.
-   **A custom domain.** Registering a personal domain and pointing it at
    GitHub Pages is a short job that can be done at any time, before or after
    the merge, and it does not change what content goes where. Section 3 notes
    where it would change the naming decision.
-   **Rewriting the ported prose.** Ported pages come across as they are, with
    dead links repaired and formatting converted. Improving the writing is a
    separate pass on a separate day, and mixing it into the migration makes it
    impossible to tell what moved from what changed.
-   **The other sites.** `synpmx`, `xgx` and `xgxr` stay where they are. They
    are already listed in `projects/projects.yml` and are linked, not absorbed.

## 2. What each site is for

|  | andrewsteinphd | TrinityMetrics |
|---|---|---|
| Subject | A person | A topic |
| Reader arrives from | A paper, a talk, a search for the name | A link to a post, GitHub |
| Reader wants | Who is this, what have they published, how do I contact them | Is this idea any good, can I use this code |
| Update rate | Yearly | Weekly to monthly |
| Built with | Google Sites | Quarto, rendered by GitHub Actions on push to `main` |

The update rates matter for placement. A publications list changes a few times
a year and a blog changes constantly, so putting them in the same listing
machinery makes the slow content look stale next to the fast content. They
should be separate listings.

The reader columns matter for the home page. Both readers land on `index.qmd`
today if the sites are merged naively, and they want different things. Section
10 handles this in the navbar rather than by writing a home page that tries to
be both.

## 3. Decision 1 --- what the site is called and what it is about

### The name

Three options, and the recommendation is A.  Andrew Stein agrees with option A.

**A. TrinityMetrics absorbs the personal site.** Title stays "TrinityMetrics",
URL stays `iamstein.github.io/TrinityMetrics/`, the person becomes a section.
Costs nothing, breaks no existing link. The objection is that a personal
site titled after a project reads oddly to someone arriving from a paper
looking for a CV, and that objection is answered by the About page opening
with the person rather than the project.

**B. Rebrand as a personal site with TrinityMetrics inside it.** Title becomes
"Andrew Stein"; TrinityMetrics becomes the name of the blog and projects
section. Truer to what the merged site is. Costs a repository rename, which
breaks `iamstein.github.io/TrinityMetrics/` and every link to it, including the
one now in `about.qmd` and any already shared. GitHub redirects a renamed
repository's git remotes; it does not redirect the Pages URL of a project site.

**C. Two Quarto projects in one repository.** Rejected. Two navbars, two
searches, two sets of styles, and a reader who crosses between them leaves one
site and enters another. This is the situation being fixed.

**Decision: A, and the domain settles it.** Andy holds `trinitymetrics.com`
and it already points at this site. The argument for B was that a custom
domain would carry a personal identity and make the repository name invisible
to readers; the domain he holds carries the project identity instead,
so it argues for A rather than against it. The site is called TrinityMetrics
because its address is TrinityMetrics.

**`site-url` is wrong and should be corrected in Phase 1.** `_quarto.yml`
declares `https://iamstein.github.io/TrinityMetrics/`. Quarto uses `site-url`
to build absolute links in the sitemap, the blog's RSS feed and the social
preview cards, so every feed entry currently advertises the `github.io`
address rather than the domain. There is also no `CNAME` file in the
repository, so how the domain is wired needs checking against the repository's
Pages settings before the value is changed.

### The three legs

**Decision: pharmacometrics, teaching and education, GenAI, in that order.**

| Leg | Holds | Already on the site as |
|---|---|---|
| Pharmacometrics | Tools and research | Projects, Code, Resources |
| Teaching and education | Pharmacometrics teaching, and guides to learning such as how to read a paper | Guides |
| GenAI | Using it in real work today | Blog |

**The joining sentence comes before the list.** Three interests listed without
a relationship read as a menu, and the relationship here is not temporal:

-   Teaching and education is how someone learns to make a defensible
    quantitative claim.
-   Pharmacometrics is making them.
-   GenAI is what happens to both when producing a *plausible* claim becomes
    cheap.

That is what earns GenAI a leg beside two lifelong practices. It acts on both
of them.

**Three durations, not three tenses.** A past / present / future reading is
available and does not hold: the guides are being written now, GenAI is in
daily use, and pharmacometrics is 17 years of past as much as it is today. The
honest version is that the legs run for different lengths of time. A lifetime
of teaching and learning, 17 years of pharmacometrics, two years of GenAI.
State the asymmetry, because it says the newest and fastest-moving of the
three is being judged by someone holding the two longest-running commitments.

**Order: pharmacometrics first.** A reader arriving from a paper wants the
professional work first, and it is the largest body of material. Teaching and
GenAI follow.

### What this rejects, and why

Recorded so the same three candidates are not re-argued later.

-   **The original modelling triad** --- mathematical analysis, biological
    modelling and storytelling, statistically supported models. It states a
    belief, which the chosen triad does not, but it has no home for the
    teaching, career and GenAI material, which is most of what is arriving.
-   **The AI triad** --- human expertise, generative AI, regulated clinical
    data. This is what `index.qmd` and `README.md` open with today. It is the
    narrowest of the candidates in the widest position, it names one leg of
    the chosen triad as though it were all three, and it is the only candidate
    tied to a technology moment rather than to a practice.
-   **The shape alone** --- that the name means three legs, none sufficient by
    itself, the failure being to mistake one for all three. True of every
    candidate and therefore not a choice between them. It survives as the
    reason the name has outlasted a change of triad, not as the home page's
    content.

Of the four, only the chosen one contains "metrics" by right, in
pharmaco**metrics**.

### What this changes

-   `index.qmd` and `README.md` both open with the AI framing and must be
    rewritten to the three legs. Phase 1.
-   The navbar in Section 10 already carries all three legs across its flat
    items, so the decision changes the home page's organizing sentence rather
    than the navigation. Whether the flat items regroup under the three legs
    is a later question, and not one to answer before the ported pages exist.
-   Teaching material in Section 4 lands by right rather than by exception.

## 4. Decision 2 --- where each kind of content lands

Presumed contents of the old site in the left column. Confirm against Section 5
once the export exists; a row with no matching page is deleted, and a page with
no matching row gets one.

| Old content | Lands at | Form |
|---|---|---|
| Home page bio | `about.qmd`, rewritten to open with the person | Prose, one screen |
| Long bio, career history | `about.qmd`, below the short bio | Prose |
| CV | Link out to the Google Doc, and publish a PDF copy fetched at build time | Link plus built file |
| Publications | `publications.qmd` driven by `publications.yml` | Listing |
| Talks, posters, slides | `talks.qmd` driven by `talks.yml`, slides as files | Listing plus files |
| Teaching, courses | `guides/`, beside the existing guides; it is a leg in its own right per Section 3 | Pages or listing entries |
| Software: xgx, xgxr, synpmx | Nothing new. Already in `projects/projects.yml` | Link out |
| Other software or code not yet listed | New rows in `projects/projects.yml` | Link out |
| Contact details | Bottom of `about.qmd` | Prose |
| News, updates | Dropped, or folded into the blog | See Section 14, Q2 |
| Photos, personal material | Case by case; record the decision in Section 5 | --- |

Two rules govern the mapping.

**A listing gets its own YAML file.** `projects/projects.yml` and
`guides/guides.yml` are the existing pattern and the new listings follow it, so
that a publication entry and a project entry are edited the same way. Section 9
covers the alternative for publications.

**A page that would hold fewer than about five entries is a section, not a
page.** Three talks do not need a Talks page in a seven-item navbar. Where the
export shows a thin section, fold it into `about.qmd` and record that in
Section 5 as a merge rather than a port.

## 6. Where the two sites already overlap

Three known overlaps, and each needs one canonical location with the other
pointing at it.

**xgx and xgxr.** Already in `projects/projects.yml`, pointing at
`opensource.nibr.com/xgx/` and the CRAN page. If the old site describes them at
length, that description does not get a second home here. Canonical: the
existing `projects.yml` rows, extended if the old descriptions say something
the current ones do not.

**The link from `about.qmd` to the old site.** `about.qmd` currently lists
Andy Stein as an author and links to
`sites.google.com/site/andrewsteinphd/home`. That link becomes self-referential
the moment the merge lands and must be removed in the same commit that
rewrites `about.qmd`.

**The bio.** Use the bio from the Google site.

## 7. Getting the content out of Google Sites

The URL shape `sites.google.com/site/...` is a Classic Sites address. Classic
Sites was retired in 2021 and surviving addresses of that shape have been
converted to new Google Sites, so treat the live site as a new Site with a
legacy URL until the export shows otherwise. The two have different export
paths.

**The route is Google Takeout, and `import_google_site.py` does the rest.**
Takeout is the only export that carries the attachments, and the attachments
are the part that cannot be reconstructed by hand.

1.  Export from [takeout.google.com](https://takeout.google.com), Sites only.
    Google emails a download link when the archive is ready.
2.  Unzip it and commit the folder to a scratch branch, `import/google-site-raw`.
    It never merges to `main`; it exists so a session can read it.
3.  Run `import_google_site.py inventory` on the unzipped folder. It prints the
    Markdown rows for Section 5, one per page and one per file, with the
    disposition columns blank and the row count at the bottom. Paste them in
    and decide the dispositions.
4.  Run `import_google_site.py convert` on the same folder. It writes one `.qmd`
    draft per page, with the site chrome removed and the front matter stubbed.
5.  Check each draft against the live page, then move it to where Section 4
    says it lands.

Steps 3 and 4 replace the transcription. What is left is the judgement: what
each page is worth, where it belongs, and what is out of date.

### How the converter avoids Google's markup

New Google Sites renders through JavaScript into deeply nested `div`s with
generated class names, so a converter that keys on those names breaks the next
time Google changes them. The script keys on nothing. It converts every page to
blocks, counts how often each block appears across all pages, and drops any
block appearing on 60% or more of them. Navigation and footers repeat by
definition; content does not. A single-page export skips the step, since there
is nothing to compare against.

The script is standard library only, with no `pandoc` and no `beautifulsoup4`,
so `python3 import_google_site.py` runs with nothing installed.

### The faster variant, if the allowlist changes

Adding `sites.google.com` to this environment's
[network allowlist](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/claude-code-on-the-web)
lets a session crawl the live site with the Chromium and Playwright already
installed here, run the same two steps, and open a pull request with the drafts
in it. That removes the export and the branch, and it lets the drafts be
checked against the live pages in the same session that writes them. It does
not replace the Takeout export: Takeout is the snapshot of the attachments and
is worth having whether or not the allowlist changes.

### What the drafts still need by hand

-   **Links between pages.** They point at old Google URLs and must be repointed
    at the new `.qmd` paths.
-   **File paths.** An image or PDF reference points into the export tree, not
    at `files/`.
-   **Front matter.** `title` is carried across; `description` and `categories`
    are stubs.
-   **Anything the converter flattened.** Multi-column layouts, embedded Google
    Drive viewers and buttons have no Markdown equivalent and come out as plain
    text or vanish. Compare against the live page.

## 8. Files and assets

Where they go: a new top-level `files/` directory, listed under `resources:` in
`_quarto.yml` so Quarto copies it into `docs/` unrendered. Existing PDFs stay
in `references/`, which is already listed there; `references/` is for the
reference documents the Resources page links, and `files/` is for the CV,
slides and posters that come across from the old site. Two directories with a
stated split beats one directory with two unrelated kinds of thing in it.

Naming: lower case, hyphens, no spaces, and a date prefix on anything with a
date attached to it, matching `blog/posts/`. `2019-acop-poster.pdf`, not
`ACoP Poster (final) v2.pdf`. A Google Sites filename usually has spaces in it,
and spaces in a URL survive but read badly and break in some link checkers.

**PDFs are the ported form for slides.** A PowerPoint file on a static site is
a download rather than a page, and a reader on a phone cannot open it. Convert
decks to PDF and keep the source file only where there is a reason to. Do not
commit the `.pptx` beside the `.pdf`: it doubles the storage, and git keeps
every version of it for the life of the repository.

### Size limits

Every presentation can live in this repository. The numbers, from GitHub's own
documentation:

| Limit | Value | Hard? |
|---|---|---|
| One file | 100 MB, with a warning at 50 MiB | Yes, the push is rejected |
| One push | 2 GB | Yes |
| Published Pages site | 1 GB | Yes |
| Pages bandwidth | 100 GB/month | Soft |
| Repository total | under 1 GB ideal, under 5 GB strongly recommended | Guidance |

The binding one is the 1 GB published site, not the 100 MB per-file limit. A
slide deck exported to PDF is nowhere near 100 MB, so no single file is at
risk; what could reach 1 GB is the sum.

### Compress every deck before committing it

Uncompressed exports are what makes the sum a problem, and Ghostscript
removes it:

```bash
gs -sDEVICE=pdfwrite -dPDFSETTINGS=/ebook -dCompatibilityLevel=1.4 \
   -dNOPAUSE -dQUIET -dBATCH -sOutputFile=out.pdf in.pdf
```

Measured on `references/Uncertainty_Assessment_Presentation.pdf`, the 105-page
deck already in this repository: 14.8 MB at source, 2.5 MB at `/ebook`, 1.5 MB
at `/screen`, page count unchanged in both. On the most image-heavy page in the
deck, `/ebook` is indistinguishable from the source and `/screen` visibly
softens the small annotation labels. **Use `/ebook`.** Re-run the comparison on
a deck of your own before trusting it on a hundred of them.

That ratio is what decides whether everything fits. At source size the 1 GB
Pages ceiling arrives at roughly 65 decks; at `/ebook` size, at roughly 400.
Compress before the first commit, because a file committed uncompressed and
recompressed later leaves both copies in the history permanently.

Git LFS is not needed. It exists for the 100 MB per-file limit, and a deck
compressed as above is 40 times smaller than that. Were it ever needed, this
repository's Actions-based Pages build could serve LFS content by setting
`lfs: true` on `actions/checkout`, which the older branch-based Pages build
could not.

### The CV is a Google Doc, and the build exports it

The CV stays in Google Docs so that editing it is the only step; nobody has to
remember to export a PDF afterwards. The build does the exporting.

A Google Doc shared as **anyone with the link, Viewer** exports over plain HTTP
with no authentication:

```
https://docs.google.com/document/d/DOC_ID/export?format=pdf
```

So `.github/workflows/publish.yml` gains one step between **Render site** and
**Upload Pages artifact**:

```yaml
      - name: Export the CV from Google Docs
        run: |
          mkdir -p docs/files
          curl --fail --silent --show-error --location \
            "https://docs.google.com/document/d/${{ vars.CV_DOC_ID }}/export?format=pdf" \
            -o docs/files/stein-cv.pdf
```

`CV_DOC_ID` is a repository variable rather than a secret, since the document
is link-shared and its ID is public in the share URL anyway.

Four properties this has:

-   **The published PDF is never stale.** It is refetched on every push to
    `main`, so it matches the Doc as of the last build.
-   **Nothing is committed.** The PDF is written into `docs/` during the build
    and travels in the Pages artifact, so it never enters git history and
    Section 8's size arithmetic is unaffected.
-   **A broken share setting fails the build.** `--fail` makes `curl` exit
    non-zero on an error response. Without it, Google's HTML error page would
    be written to `stein-cv.pdf` and published as a corrupt file, which is the
    failure nobody notices.
-   **The reader never meets Google.** The site links its own
    `files/stein-cv.pdf`, so there is no account prompt, no Drive viewer, and
    no dependency on Google being up when someone opens the CV. Offer the Doc
    link beside it only if there is a reason to.

The export endpoint is not part of a documented API and Google could change it.
The build failing loudly is the detection mechanism; the fallback is to commit
a PDF by hand until it is fixed.

## 9. Publications: how the list is built

Two options.

**A. A YAML file plus a Quarto listing**, matching `projects.yml` and
`guides.yml`. Each entry carries title, authors, journal, year, DOI, and a link.
Consistent with everything else on this site, editable without a toolchain, and
the listing gives sorting and categories.

**B. A BibTeX file rendered through Quarto's citation support.** Correct
formatting for free, exports cleanly for anyone who wants to cite the work, and
`.bib` can be exported from Google Scholar in one step rather than typed.

**Recommendation: A, with the `.bib` file committed alongside it as a
download.** The YAML drives what a reader sees, so the page looks like the rest
of the site and can carry a note on a paper where a note is useful. The `.bib`
serves the reader who wants to cite something and costs one export to produce.
The duplication is real and is the price; it is bounded by publications being
added a few times a year, one entry at a time.

Do not hand-type the publication list. Export from the Google Scholar profile,
then check it, because Scholar merges and mis-attributes entries and a
publication list with someone else's paper in it is worse than a short one.

## 10. Navigation after the merge

The navbar has seven left-hand items now and the merge adds at least three.
Ten flat items do not fit on a laptop width and do not survive on a phone.

Proposed structure:

```
Home | Blog | Projects | Guides | Resources | Code | About ▾
                                                      ├─ About
                                                      ├─ CV  (→ Google Docs)
                                                      ├─ Publications
                                                      └─ Talks
```

The CV entry is an external link, per Section 4. Quarto takes a full URL in a
navbar `href`, so it needs no page of its own.

The person's material sits under one menu, the topic material stays flat, and
the site's shape barely changes for a reader who is already using it. A reader
arriving from a paper looks for a name, finds About, and everything about the
person is one click below it.

The alternative, a second navbar row or a `right:` group, splits the navigation
into two zones and asks the reader to work out what the split means.

**The home page stays as it is.** `index.qmd` frames the project and links to
the five sections. It gains one line pointing at About for the reader who came
for the person. It does not become a personal landing page; Section 3 chose
the project as the site's identity and the home page is where that choice is
visible.

## 11. Old URLs and inbound links

Every old URL breaks unless something is done, and the ones that matter are the
ones printed in places that cannot be edited: papers, conference bios, slide
footers, the Google Scholar profile, other people's link lists.

**Google Sites cannot redirect to an external site.** There is no redirect
feature and no server to configure. The workable substitute is to keep the old
site published and replace each page's body with a short pointer to the new
address, page by page, matching the Section 5 inventory. A reader following a
ten-year-old citation lands on a live page that tells them where to go.

**Do not delete the old site.** Not at the end of the migration, not a year
later. It costs nothing to leave a Google Site published and it is the only
thing standing between an old citation and a 404.

**Files need pointers too.** A PDF cannot carry a pointer. Where a file's old
URL is likely to be cited, replace the attachment with a one-page PDF giving
the new address, or leave the original in place and accept that the two copies
diverge. Decide per row in Section 5.

**Update what can be updated.** The Google Scholar profile's homepage field,
the GitHub profile, LinkedIn, ORCID, and any conference bio still within reach.
This is a short list and it catches most live traffic.

## 12. Acceptance checks

The migration is done when all of these hold.

1.  Every row of the Section 5 inventory has a disposition, and every DROP row
    has a reason.
2.  The number of pages and files ported plus merged plus linked plus dropped
    equals the row count recorded in Section 5.
3.  A link checker over the rendered `docs/` reports no broken internal links.
    `quarto render` then a link checker over the output; `lychee` or
    `linkchecker` will do.
4.  No page on the merged site links to `sites.google.com/site/andrewsteinphd`
    as a live destination. `grep -r andrewsteinphd` returns hits only inside
    `projects/site-integration/`, where the old address is the subject rather
    than a reference.
5.  Every file referenced from a ported page exists under `files/` or
    `references/` and is listed under `resources:` in `_quarto.yml`.
6.  Every page on the old site shows either its original content or a pointer
    to the new address. No page is left half-migrated.
7.  The site renders and publishes from `.github/workflows/publish.yml` without
    manual steps.

## 13. Sequence

Phases are ordered so that each one leaves the site in a publishable state.
None of them requires the next one to start.

**Phase 0 --- inventory.** Take the Takeout export, commit it to
`import/google-site-raw`, and run `import_google_site.py inventory` to generate
the Section 5 rows. Decide the dispositions and record the row count. Answer
the open questions in Section 14 that the export settles. This phase produces
no site change and it is the phase that makes the rest estimable. Do not skip
it and port pages as they are noticed; that is how a page gets left behind.

**Phase 1 --- the person, at minimum.** Rewrite `about.qmd` to open with the
bio from the Google site and remove the self-referential link. Add the CV
export step to `publish.yml` and set the `CV_DOC_ID` variable. Correct
`site-url` to the domain. Rewrite `index.qmd` and `README.md` to the three
legs in Section 3. Add the About menu from Section 10. After this
phase the merged site
already answers "who is this" and the old site is optional rather than load
bearing.

**Phase 2 --- publications and talks.** Add `publications.yml`,
`publications.qmd`, the `.bib`, and the same for talks if the volume in Section
5 justifies a page. Copy slides and posters into `files/`.

**Phase 3 --- everything else.** The remaining PORT and MERGE rows. Extend
`projects/projects.yml` with any software the old site lists that this one does
not.

**Phase 4 --- the old site becomes pointers.** Only after Phases 1 to 3 are
published and checked. Replace each old page's body with its pointer, and
update the external profiles listed in Section 11.

**Phase 5 --- acceptance.** Run Section 12 end to end and record the result at
the bottom of Section 5.
